I'll write about something that's been on my mind lately: the strange intimacy of watching strangers' lives through apartment windows in dense cities.

---

The Ethics of Looking Sideways

I live on the fourth floor of a building in a neighborhood where the buildings are close enough that I can see into perhaps thirty other apartments without leaving my couch. This is not unique. Millions of people in cities worldwide exist in this same condition of overlapping privacy, separated by air and glass and the unspoken agreement that we will pretend not to see each other.

But we do see. Of course we do.

My neighbor across the narrow courtyard—I'll call her the woman in yellow, though I've never learned her name—has a kitchen window directly aligned with my living room. For two years, I've watched her make coffee every morning at 6:47, the time so consistent that I've used her appearance as a backup alarm. She wears a yellow robe that has faded noticeably since I first noticed her. She stirs her coffee with the spoon handle pointed outward, three times, always three. She reads something on her phone, her face illuminated from below, and sometimes she smiles, sometimes she doesn't. I know nothing about her. I know these rituals intimately.

There's a older couple on the third floor of the building to my left. They fight sometimes, not loudly, but with the theatrical gestures of people who have been performing conflict for decades. He throws his hands up. She turns her back. They always reconcile within the same evening, always with tea. I've never heard their voices, only watched this silent cinema. During the pandemic, I worried about them with an intensity that surprised me. When their lights went out early, I assumed illness. When they stayed up late, I felt relief. Strangers, and I was monitoring their sleep patterns.

The young man on the top floor to my right practices saxophone badly. I mean this affectionately. He plays "Careless Whisper" approximately four times per week, never improving, never quite hitting that one note. I find myself listening for him, disappointed when he skips a day. During summer, when windows open, the sound drifts across, fractured and beautiful in its persistence. I want to applaud when he finishes. I never have.

What strikes me about this arrangement is how thoroughly we've normalized it. We draw our curtains when we need true privacy, but mostly we live in these illuminated dioramas, visible to anyone who happens to look. We cook, argue, dance alone, cry, exercise, exist in these boxes with one wall made of transparent material, and we trust—what? That the sheer number of other windows makes us unremarkable? That looking is understood to be impolite, so no one will do it? The math doesn't work. Someone is always looking. I am always looking.

I've developed theories about the ethics of this. Passive observation feels different from active surveillance. I don't use binoculars. I don't record. I don't tell others what I've seen. The information goes nowhere, dies with my attention. But this justification is suspiciously convenient, isn't it? "I only looked, I didn't *do* anything with it." The looking itself is doing something. It changes me. It creates relationships that exist in only one direction, which is a kind of violence, or a kind of love, or both.

The philosopher Emmanuel Levinas wrote about the face of the Other, how encountering another person's face creates an ethical demand, a responsibility. But what about the face seen at distance, unaware, unencountered? Does the ethical demand still apply when the other doesn't know they're being faced? I think it might apply doubly, because the one-directional nature of the gaze means all the responsibility sits with the looker. They cannot meet me halfway. They don't know there's a path to meet on.

I tried an experiment last year. I started waving at the woman in yellow. Just a small raise of my hand when I saw her at her kitchen window. The first time, she didn't respond. The second time, she looked confused, then looked away. The third time, she waved back, a tiny motion, and immediately drew her curtain. It stayed drawn for three days. I felt like I'd broken something, committed a category error. The fourth day, the curtain was open again, and we resumed our previous arrangement: her making coffee, me watching, neither acknowledging the other. The wave had been too much, too real. We needed the fiction of invisibility to continue our visible intimacy.

There's a word in Japanese, *kataomoi*, that means unrequited love, but literally translates to "one-sided love." I've come to think my relationships with these visible strangers are something like kataomoi, but stripped of romance. One-sided knowing. One-sided care. One-sided grief when someone moves away and their window goes dark and new people arrive with new rituals I must learn from nothing.

The saxophone player stopped playing three months ago. I don't know why. Maybe he moved. Maybe he got better and now plays only in venues I'll never enter. Maybe he gave up. I watch his window now, hoping for the return of bad George Michael covers, aware that I have no right to this hope, no standing to miss him. But I do. I miss the sound of someone trying, failing, trying again, audible evidence of human persistence floating across the gap between buildings, between lives that will never properly touch.

I think this is what cities really are: not collections of buildings, but these networks of peripheral vision, these accumulated almost-connections. We are alone together in ways that previous generations, living in villages or scattered homesteads, could not have imagined. The medieval peasant knew everyone they saw. The suburbanite knows their neighbors, at least by name. The urban apartment dweller knows the silhouette of a stranger's morning routine, the rhythm of their light switches, the color of their curtains, and nothing else. A new form of human relationship, unnamed, unacknowledged, perhaps not healthy but undeniably real.

I should probably stop watching. I won't. The woman in yellow just appeared in her kitchen, yellow robe more faded than ever, stirring her coffee three times with the handle outward. I don't wave. She doesn't look up. The day begins, and we continue our strange shared solitude, separated by everything and nothing, intimate strangers in the architecture of modern life.

---
